Memory Jogger.new: A Wisconsin county social-services agency repeatedly documented signs that four-year-old Joshua DeShaney was being abused by his father but never removed him; the Court held 6--3 that the Due Process Clause imposes no duty to protect against private violence unless the State has taken the person into custody or created the danger (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/489/189/}{Justia}).

Judicial Votes.new: The Supreme Court \textbf{affirmed} the Seventh Circuit by a \textbf{6--3} vote. The case was argued November 2, 1988, and decided February 22, 1989 (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/489/189/}{Justia}; \href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/489/189}{Cornell LII}):

Analysis of Opinions.new: \subsubsection{State Tort Law and the Social-Worker Dilemma}

Analysis of Opinions.src: The Supreme Court reinforced this boundary in \href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/503/115}{\textit{Collins v. City of Harker Heights}, 503 U.S. 115 (1992)} (no substantive due process duty to provide municipal employees a safe workplace), and closed the procedural-entitlement loophole left open in \textit{DeShaney}'s footnote 2 in \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/545/748/}{\textit{Town of Castle Rock v. Gonzales}, 545 U.S. 748 (2005)}, holding that even a seemingly mandatory state domestic-violence restraining-order statute confers no constitutionally protected ``property'' interest in police enforcement.

Meanwhile, Chief Justice Rehnquist's observation that Wisconsin ``played no part in [the dangers'] creation, nor did it do anything to render him any more vulnerable to them'' (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/489/189/}{489 U.S. at 201}) spawned the federal circuits' \textbf{state-created danger} doctrine. Most federal courts of appeals recognize substantive due process liability when a state actor affirmatively creates or enhances a foreseeable risk of private harm with conscience-shocking culpability, though the Supreme Court has never formally endorsed the doctrine and circuit tests diverge sharply (\href{https://lawreview.uchicago.edu/online-archive/exploring-statutory-remedies-state-created-dangers-after-fisher-v-moore}{U. Chi. L. Rev. Online}).

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (State Prevails): Slow Response to Protective-Order Violations.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: City police receive three 911 calls reporting that a local resident is threatening his estranged spouse outside her apartment in violation of a state protective order. Dispatch logs the calls as low priority, no patrol car arrives for two hours, and the resident assaults the spouse. Under \textit{DeShaney} and \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/545/748/}{\textit{Castle Rock}}, a \S~1983 Due Process suit fails: the victim was not in state custody, police did not affirmatively create the danger, and state protective-order statutes confer no federal procedural property interest in arrest (remedies lie, if at all, in state tort law or Equal Protection if non-enforcement was discriminatory).

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (State Prevails): Broken Promises of Extra Patrols.} A woman tells her local police department that a former boyfriend has threatened to kill her. An officer promises that patrol cars will drive past her house every hour that week, but none do, and on the third night the former boyfriend breaks in and injures her. She sues the officer and the city under \S~1983, arguing that the promise created a special relationship. Under \textit{DeShaney}, the claim fails. The State did not restrain her liberty, and the danger came from a private actor. The Court made clear that an affirmative duty arises not from the State's knowledge of a person's predicament or its ``expressions of intent to help him,'' but only from limits it has imposed on the person's freedom to act on her own behalf. Any remedy lies in state tort law (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/489/189/}{Justia}).
\item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Plaintiff Prevails): A Child Stranded on the Highway.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: After arresting an intoxicated driver at 1:00 a.m. in sub-freezing weather on an unlit rural interstate, a state trooper confiscates the car keys and orders the driver's sober seven-year-old passenger out of the car to ``walk home'' along the highway shoulder rather than waiting for a guardian. The child is struck by a passing motorist.

Unlike \textit{DeShaney}, the officer did not merely stand by while a preexisting private danger unfolded. By affirmatively removing the child from a safe vehicle and stranding her in an exposed, lethal environment she could not escape, the state actor affirmatively created the peril and rendered the child far more vulnerable to harm (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/489/189/}{489 U.S. at 201}; cf. \textit{White v. Rochford}, 592 F.2d 381 (7th Cir. 1979)). In circuits recognizing state-created danger (and arguably as a brief custodial deprivation of liberty), the plaintiff states a viable substantive due process claim.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Custody Triggers a Duty): A Prisoner Beaten by a Cellmate.} A state prisoner tells prison officers that his cellmate has threatened to kill him and asks to be moved. The officers laugh off the request, and that night the cellmate beats him severely. Unlike Joshua, the prisoner is in state custody: the State has locked him in a cell with his attacker and taken away his ability to protect himself or seek help. \textit{DeShaney} itself explained that when the State so restrains a person's liberty, as in \textit{Estelle v.\ Gamble} and \textit{Youngberg v.\ Romeo}, it assumes a duty to provide for his basic needs, including reasonable safety. The prisoner can state a constitutional claim if he shows the officers knew of and disregarded a substantial risk to his safety, the Eighth Amendment standard the Court applied to prisoners attacked by other inmates in \textit{Farmer v.\ Brennan}, 511 U.S.\ 825 (1994).

\item \textbf{Fence-Sitter (Foster Care): Abuse in a State-Selected Foster Home.} A county child-welfare agency removes a six-year-old from her parents and places her with foster parents it has licensed and supervises. Caseworkers receive two reports that the foster father is hitting her but do not investigate, and she is seriously injured. The agency relies on \textit{DeShaney}: the abuser was a private person, not a state employee. The child answers that the State took her from her family and chose where she would live, a restraint on her liberty much closer to institutionalization than Joshua's situation. \textit{DeShaney} expressly left open whether a child in state-arranged foster care stands in a custodial relationship with the State (489 U.S.\ at 201 n.9), and the Supreme Court has not resolved the question, so the outcome is uncertain.

Key Quotations.src: ``The Clause is phrased as a limitation on the State's power to act, not as a guarantee of certain minimal levels of safety and security. It forbids the State itself to deprive individuals of life, liberty, or property without `due process of law,' but its language cannot fairly be extended to impose an affirmative obligation on the State to ensure that those interests do not come to harm through other means. . . . Its purpose was to protect the people from the State, not to ensure that the State protected them from each other.''

Key Quotations.new: --- Chief Justice Rehnquist, for the Court,

Key Quotations.src: ``The affirmative duty to protect arises not from the State's knowledge of the individual's predicament or from its expressions of intent to help him, but from the limitation which it has imposed on his freedom to act on his own behalf.''

Key Quotations.new: --- Chief Justice Rehnquist, for the Court,

Key Quotations.src: ``While the State may have been aware of the dangers that Joshua faced in the free world, it played no part in their creation, nor did it do anything to render him any more vulnerable to them.''

Key Quotations.new: --- Chief Justice Rehnquist, for the Court,

Key Quotations.src: ``Poor Joshua! Victim of repeated attacks by an irresponsible, bullying, cowardly, and intemperate father, and abandoned by respondents, who placed him in a dangerous predicament and who knew or learned what was going on, and yet did essentially nothing except, as the Court revealingly observes, \textit{ante} at 193, `dutifully recorded these incidents in [their] files.'''
